full_judgment:
51. The submission that (i) defence does not owe any legal obligation to make out a case at least by way of suggestion to the witnesses in any event; (ii) in order to support a plea of mutiny, no condition precedent that army officers involved in the mutiny would have to submit their charter of demand to the authority of the armed forces is necessarily essential; (iii) intended mutiny in the least is also a mutiny as per section 31 of the Army Act, 1952 and section 36 of the Navy Ordinance, 1961 and mutiny committed and intended or absence of mutiny is to be deduced from the facts and circumstances of the case on record but not on any assumption; (iv)onus of proof as attributed to the above findings to the shoulder of the defence has been shifted illegally; (v) in the cumulative result of the above, error of law apparent on the face of the record has been caused occasioning failure of justice are based upon misconception of law. 

 61. This Court on assessment on the evidence on record particularly the evidence of Md. Arninur Rahman (PW 24) Md. Rezaul Huq, (PW 37), Shafayet Jamil (PW 44) observed that the defence specifically did not raise the plea of the mutiny by way of cross-examination or by giving suggestion to the witnesses, rather the evidence on record revealed that the killers of the President were rewarded instead of putting them on trial for the alleged charge of mutiny for killing the President and thus the authority in power justified their act. The accused persons raised this point for the first time in the High Court Division. In his written argument Mr. Khan Saifur Rahman argued "but the evidence and materials on record show that the criminal conspiracy involved mutiny to change the then Mujib Government. In this connection it may be noticed that any allegation of mutiny carries with it the existence of conspiracy within the definition of the offence of mutiny." In this written argument learned Counsel impliedly admitted on behalf of his clients that the accused in Criminal Appeal Nos.56 of 2007 and 58 of 2007 were involved in criminal conspiracy to commit mutiny. In view of this submission this court observed that the accused having admitted their act as criminal conspiracy to commit mutiny, in the absence of proof of 'mutiny', an adverse inference could have been drawn that the accused per- sons involved in conspiracy to commit the murder. Therefore, I find no basis in the contention of the learned counsel that there are inconsistent findings in the judgment of this court. 

 62. This court observed that though the prosecution is required to prove the charges leveled against the accused beyond reasonable doubt and the defence is not required prove anything in sup- port of its case, but in the context of defense's admission an adverse inference may be drawn that the accused hatched up criminal conspiracy to commit the murder of the President. True, the burden is always with the prosecution to prove its case. But in certain circumstances the burden also lies on the accused to make out that his case comes under any one of the exceptions. Section 105 of the Evidence Act says nothing about pleas; it merely places the burden of proof in certain circumstances on an accused person. Since the burden of the general issue is on the prosecution from beginning to end, the provisions of section 105 must be under stood in the special sense that while all the details of a criminal transaction are relevant to the case for the prosecution as being part of resgestae, and must be proved by the prosecution, yet the prosecution is under no duty to exclude the defence which are open to the accused person, or to furnish proof of facts of a special nature having relevance only to the particular defence which the accused sets up. The burden that cast on the accused in a criminal case by virtue of this section, no doubt, is not so onerous as the primary burden cast on the prosecution to prove the offence beyond reasonable doubt. It is sufficient, if the accused, who pleads a fact in support of his defence, satisfies the court of the probability of what he has been called upon to establish, and if on the evidence, it appears probable that the defence set up is true, he is entitled to a decision in his favour, even though be may not have succeeded in proving the truth of his version beyond reasonable doubt. 

 63. Section 106 of the Evidence Act enacts the second exception to the general rule that the burden of proof is on a party who asserts the affirmative of a fact. Under this rule, the burden of proof lies on the person who wishes to support his case by a particular fact which lies more particularly within his knowledge. The rule is of general application; it holds good whether the proof of the issue involves the proof of an affirmative or of negative, and has been allowed to prevail against presumption of law. The true purpose of this section is discernible from the first illustration that when a person does an act with some intention other than that which the character and circumstances of the act suggest the burden proving that intention is upon him. It is only in cases where the facts proved by the evidence give rise to a reasonable. inference of guilt unless the same is rebutted, that such inference can be negatived by proof of some fact which, in its nature, can only be within the special knowledge of the accused.
